clinicalPearls: Presents in early infancy with profound neutropenia and recurrent, often severe, bacterial infections such as omphalitis, skin abscesses, and pneumonia
Autosomal dominant ELANE mutations are the commonest cause, whereas classic autosomal recessive Kostmann syndrome results from HAX1 mutations
The marrow characteristically shows maturation arrest of the myeloid series at the promyelocyte or myelocyte stage
Most patients respond to granulocyte colony-stimulating factor (G-CSF), which raises neutrophil counts and reduces infection
There is a lifelong risk of clonal evolution to myelodysplastic syndrome and acute myeloid leukaemia, often heralded by acquired CSF3R and RUNX1 mutations
Haematopoietic stem cell transplantation is the definitive option for G-CSF-refractory disease or when leukaemic transformation supervenes
Diagnosis combines persistent severe neutropenia, marrow maturation arrest, and targeted genetic testing while excluding autoimmune and secondary causes
reference.pathophysiology: Severe congenital neutropenia is a group of inherited disorders of granulopoiesis in which neutrophil precursors fail to mature. ELANE mutations produce a misfolded neutrophil elastase that triggers the unfolded protein response and endoplasmic reticulum stress, driving apoptosis of promyelocytes; HAX1 mutations remove a protein that maintains mitochondrial membrane potential, again promoting precursor apoptosis. Other genes converge on similar pathways of accelerated myeloid progenitor death or defective intracellular trafficking. The net effect is arrest of myeloid maturation with near-absent circulating neutrophils. Chronic G-CSF stimulation of a genetically unstable myeloid compartment, together with acquisition of CSF3R and other somatic mutations, underlies the elevated risk of transformation to myelodysplasia and acute myeloid leukaemia.
additionalDifferentials: Glycogen storage disease type Ib and other metabolic neutropenias
Reticular dysgenesis and other combined immunodeficiencies
additionalInvestigations: Serial full blood counts to confirm persistent severe neutropenia and distinguish from cyclic disease
Bone marrow aspirate and trephine to demonstrate myeloid maturation arrest
Targeted genetic panel (ELANE, HAX1, and other SCN genes)
Antineutrophil antibody testing to exclude autoimmune neutropenia
Cytogenetics and serial marrow surveillance for CSF3R/RUNX1 mutations and MDS/AML evolution
Immunological workup where a syndromic or combined immunodeficiency is suspected
redFlags: Recurrent life-threatening bacterial or fungal infection with an absolute neutrophil count persistently very low
New cytogenetic abnormality, rising blasts, or acquired CSF3R/RUNX1 mutation signalling leukaemic transformation
Escalating G-CSF requirement with declining response
Sepsis or deep-seated infection in a febrile neutropenic infant requiring urgent broad-spectrum cover
reference.prognosis: G-CSF has transformed survival by controlling infection, but patients carry a substantial lifelong risk of transformation to myelodysplasia and acute myeloid leukaemia, so surveillance is essential and transplantation is curative for high-risk or refractory disease.
pitfalls: Mistaking severe congenital neutropenia for autoimmune neutropenia and delaying G-CSF
Failing to perform serial marrow surveillance and missing early clonal evolution
Attributing a poor G-CSF response solely to under-dosing rather than considering transformation
Overlooking syndromic features that point to a specific genetic diagnosis
references: Nathan and Oski's Hematology and Oncology of Infancy and Childhood
management: Granulocyte colony-stimulating factor (G-CSF) as first-line therapy to raise neutrophil counts and reduce infections
Prompt broad-spectrum antibiotics for febrile or bacterial infection, with meticulous skin and oral hygiene
Haematopoietic stem cell transplantation for G-CSF-refractory disease or on leukaemic transformation
Surveillance for clonal evolution with serial marrow examination and cytogenetics, watching for acquired CSF3R and RUNX1 mutations
Monitor full blood count response and titrate G-CSF to the lowest effective level
Genetic counselling and family testing given the heritable ELANE and HAX1 basis
Escalate to transplantation on emergence of myelodysplasia or acute myeloid leukaemia
Coordinate long-term care through a haematology multidisciplinary team
